outcome: The general conjecture (no three consecutive powerful integers exist) remains open, but several papers since March 2025 have ruled out specific structural families of hypothetical counterexamples centered on a perfect cube (e.g. middle term a perfect cube with the outer terms of restricted prime-power shapes), narrowing where a counterexample could hide.

ai.basis_quote: In the making of this paper, ChatGPT was used as a sounding board, for proofreading and for supplying numerical examples, most notably the calculation of the recurrence relation (4) in Section 3.2 and Table 1 in Section 5.3. The paper itself was entirely human-generated.

summary: The Erdős–Mollin–Walsh conjecture (no three consecutive powerful integers) is still open in general, but the window since 26 Jan 2024 saw a genuine sequence of case-settling results, consistent with the triage's 'likely' verdict. Tsz Ho Chan's note (arXiv:2503.21485, submitted 27 Mar 2025; published as INTEGERS 25 (2025) #A7, received 17 Oct 2024, accepted 7 Jan 2025) proved nonexistence of consecutive powerful triples where the middle term is a perfect cube and each outer term has only a single prime factor to an odd power, using Pell equations, elliptic curves and second-order recurrences — this is a genuine restriction (case) of the original all-quantified conjecture, so it counts as `partial` per §3.1. Jialai She's arXiv:2507.16828 (v1 7 Jul 2025, revised through v3 24 Sep 2025) extended this to eliminate a further family centered on cubes with prime-square factors, using modular arithmetic, p-adic valuation, Thue equations and elliptic curves. A third paper, Wenjun Ma's arXiv:2608.23418 (24 Aug 2026), explicitly built on Chan's result and generalized the cube-centered nonexistence result to allow the middle term to be any perfect power (not just a cube) for infinitely many exponents n ≡ 5 mod 8 in the relevant sense, again a restriction/case rather than the full statement. All three papers are recent preprints (Chan's is also journal-published in INTEGERS, a refereed venue, so that specific case is `resolved`-grade, but since the record covers the conjecture as a whole and the general statement is untouched, `partial` is the correct overall status per §6.1). None of these three papers disclose any AI system in their methodology or acknowledgements — I opened all of them (PDF/HTML) and found no such statements. I did find AI disclosure in a related but distinct paper, Wouter van Doorn's arXiv:2605.06697 ('Three-term arithmetic progressions of consecutive powerful numbers', submitted 4 May 2026), which states ChatGPT was used 'as a sounding board, for proofreading and for supplying numerical examples' and that 'the paper itself was entirely human-generated.' That paper does not settle a case of the Erdős–Mollin–Walsh conjecture itself — it proves existence of 3-term APs of powerful numbers with small common difference and separately conjectures (unproven) that infinitely many such APs are of *consecutive* integers, which if true would answer a different, weaker Erdős question (on powerful numbers in AP, tracked as erdosproblems.com #938) in the negative; it does not bear on whether three *consecutive integers* can all be powerful in the way the frozen bullet asks, so per §3.1 this is a related problem, not a case, and is mentioned only for completeness, not counted as an event. Even if it had been in scope, the ChatGPT usage (proofreading, generating numerical examples/table entries for illustration) matches the enumerated `none` exclusions in §6.2 verbatim, not `assisted`. I also checked erdosproblems.com's own entry for this exact conjecture (problem #364, maintained by Terence Tao's team), which independently confirms the conjecture is open and credits exactly Chan (2025) and She (2025) for the same two partial results, with no AI system credited. A Quanta Magazine article on 'Why the Legendary Erdős Problems Are Falling to AI' (Aug 2026) surveys several AI-assisted Erdős-problem resolutions (unit distance problem, problems 333, 728, 1102, 1196) but does not mention the Erdős–Mollin–Walsh conjecture or problem #364 at all, corroborating that AI involvement has not reached this particular problem.
competing_reading: One could argue the overall status should be `resolved` for Chan's specific sub-case in isolation since it is peer-reviewed and expert-digested (via INTEGERS and the erdosproblems.com database), but because the record is scoped to the conjecture as stated in the bullet ('no three consecutive numbers are all powerful' — the fully general statement), and that general statement is untouched, `partial` is the more faithful single status. Also arguable: whether Ma's Aug 2026 paper (allowing the middle term to be any sufficiently structured perfect power, not just a cube) is a strictly larger case-elimination than Chan's original cube-only result or a genuinely separate family; either way it is still a `partial` case, not a full resolution, so this does not change the status.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof via an explicit counterexample) covering all three consecutive integers without restricting to special structural families (cube-centered middle terms, restricted prime-power shapes, etc.) would resolve the conjecture outright. Short of that, tracking erdosproblems.com #364 and future arXiv submissions citing Chan/She/Ma is the way to see further case-elimination.
